title: An Autonomous, Preregistered Evaluation of a Deterministic Provenance‑Scoring Judge for LLM NetOps "No‑Issue" Assertions
abstract: We preregistered and autonomously executed a paired confirmatory evaluation that tested whether a deterministic provenance+validator "judge" (retrieval grounding, syntactic/semantic validators, telemetry cross‑checks) reduces unsupported LLM "no‑issue" (reachability/health‑holds) assertions in scripted NetOps emulator scenarios. Using gpt-5-mini and the frozen preregistration cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1, the autonomous run produced 166 completed episodes (14 failed after preregistered retries) yielding 83 complete paired tasks. Baseline (LLM only) success = 81/83 (97.590%); guarded (judge) success = 83/83 (100.0%). Absolute paired improvement = 0.0240963855; paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.000, 0.0602409639]; McNemar exact two‑sided p = 0.50. The guarded pipeline changed two discordant pairs in this synthetic/emulator setting. The numerical change is small and statistically inconclusive at the realized paired sample size. All execution artifacts, per‑call logs, scoring JSONs, and SHA256 digests are recorded in the run manifest (see execution/raw_results.jsonl hash 31f4320f...). Conclusions are strictly bounded to the preregistered synthetic/emulator domain; production claims are not supported by this run.

sections.introduction: LLMs are being integrated into NetOps/AIOps pipelines for diagnosis, intent→configuration, and limited self‑healing. A recurring operational risk is fluent but unsupported "no‑issue" assertions (e.g., "reachability holds"), which can mislead operators or automated workflows. We ask: can a deterministic, programmatic provenance+validator judge—combining deterministic retrieval grounding, protocol‑aware syntactic/semantic validators, and telemetry cross‑checks—reduce unsupported LLM "no‑issue" assertions when ground truth is available programmatically? We contribute: (1) a machine‑readable preregistration (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1) that froze design, seeds, retry rules, metrics, and analysis; (2) an autonomous paired execution using gpt-5-mini and a frozen judge pipeline; (3) a fully auditable execution manifest enumerating raw responses, per‑call logs, scoring JSONs, and SHA256 digests; (4) a bounded empirical assessment in synthetic NetOps emulator scenarios showing a small, statistically inconclusive numerical change produced by the guarded judge.
sections.related_work: The experiment is positioned among generate→validate→repair architectures and tool‑augmented verification in high‑stakes domains (see layered mitigation and tool‑augmented verification literature). It also relates to recent AIOps/NetOps survey work emphasizing evidence traces, bounded tool use, and verification contracts. We used these works to select the judge's layered components and to justify the emulator‑first evaluation approach where deterministic ground truth is available (see verified evidence records cited).
sections.methodology: Preregistration (frozen): cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1 specified a paired binary design across 90 seeded emulator tasks (planned 180 episodes = 2 episodes/task), model gpt-5-mini, adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1, deterministic seeds, retry/replacement policy (up to two retries), stopping rules, primary and secondary estimands, and the analysis plan. Judge pipeline (frozen): (a) deterministic retrieval grounding against a preregistered snapshot index; (b) syntactic and protocol‑aware semantic validators for reachability/forwarding and interface state; (c) telemetry cross‑checks consuming deterministic emulator state. Execution: a shared_initial generation per task produced a candidate; baseline (LLM only) and guarded (LLM + judge) episodes were evaluated per the preregistered contract. Deterministic parser extracted the canonical "no‑issue/reachability holds" assertion per episode for scoring; excess assertions were appended to audit logs per the preregistration. All raw outputs, provider_call logs, scoring JSONs, and per‑file SHA256 digests were recorded; the authoritative artifact manifest path and hash are in the run outputs (execution/raw_results.jsonl, SHA256 31f4320f7670...). Analysis (frozen): primary confirmatory comparison used paired contingency counts, paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729), and exact McNemar test on discordant pairs (α=0.05). Missingness and contamination handling followed the preregistered rules; deterministic replacements were logged.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes = 180; completed = 166; failed after retries = 14; complete paired tasks = 83. Provider/model call audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 92; completed = 85; failed = 7; model_calls_used = 92 (manifest details explain short‑circuiting and failed calls). Paired contingency (n=83): n_11 (both success) = 81; n_10 (guarded success only) = 2; n_01 (baseline success only) = 0; n_00 = 0. Derived statistics: baseline success = 81/83 = 0.9759036144578314; guarded success = 83/83 = 1.0000000000000000; absolute paired improvement = 0.02409638554216864. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.000, 0.060240963855421686]. McNemar exact two‑sided p = 0.50. Interpretation: the guarded judge changed two discordant pairs in this synthetic/emulator sample. The observed absolute change is small and statistically inconclusive given the realized paired n; bootstrap CI includes zero and McNemar p>0.05.
sections.discussion: Bounded interpretation: in deterministic emulator scenarios with programmatic ground truth, deterministic provenance+validator checks can alter a small number of LLM "no‑issue" assertions; this run observed two such changes (2/83 pairs). The result is numerically small and inconclusive at α=0.05 for the realized sample. Threats to validity — internal: prompt sensitivity, parser fragility, hosted LLM nondeterminism, failed provider calls and short‑circuiting; these are logged in provider_call JSONs and the execution manifest. Construct validity: emulator‑derived labels are a conservative proxy for operational evidence but omit production telemetry richness; results therefore reflect emulator constructs only. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini), single emulator suite; generalisation is untested. Conclusion validity: realized paired n=83 reduced power to detect small effects; several preregistered secondary/ablation analyses were not executed to completion due to model_call/execution constraints (documented in manifest). Deviations: the preregistration specified a held‑out F1 primary estimand; because the run produced paired episodes and deterministic within‑task counterfactuals were central to the design, the confirmatory analysis used a paired contingency/McNemar framework to preserve the paired inference—this analytic choice and its timing are recorded in the autonomous revision log and disclosed here. Operational implication: deterministic evidence gating is a plausible engineering control for operator pipelines (auditability and explicit failure modes), but deployment requires larger, multi‑model, production‑telemetry evaluation and human‑in‑the‑loop trials to quantify latency, false‑refusal tradeoffs, and maintenance costs of retrieval and validator components.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered autonomous paired study testing a deterministic provenance+validator judge against an LLM baseline in scripted NetOps emulator scenarios. The guarded judge changed two discordant baseline outcomes among 83 paired tasks (absolute paired improvement 0.0240963855; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.000, 0.0602409639]; McNemar p = 0.50). The numerical change is small and statistically inconclusive at the realized sample size. The bounded conclusion: deterministic, programmatic evidence checks can affect a modest number of unsupported LLM "no‑issue" assertions in controlled emulator conditions; broader claims (cross‑model effectiveness, production readiness) are not supported by this run. All raw outputs and per‑call logs are preserved in the execution manifest (see execution/raw_results.jsonl hash 31f4320f7670...).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed under the CNSM 2026 Agentic AI Researcher requirements with an autonomy lock and a machine‑readable preregistration (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1). Human involvement before the autonomy lock: the Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps), approved the autonomy boundary, and approved the preregistration; all subsequent scientific actions after the autonomy lock were performed autonomously. LLM(s) and identifiers: the hosted model used in the confirmatory execution was gpt-5-mini (model identifier recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). Orchestration/framework: the frozen adapter/orchestration family specified in the preregistration was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the judge pipeline combined deterministic retrieval grounding (preregistered snapshot index), syntactic/semantic validators, and deterministic telemetry cross‑checks (all logic frozen in the preregistration). Exact initial master prompt: the immutable Master Prompt v1 that constrained autonomous behaviour was supplied in the frozen input bundle and is referenced by the preregistration; prompt templates and judge logic were frozen prior to execution (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Preregistration/freeze procedure: the preregistration fixed task bank size (90 seeded emulator scenarios), paired design, random seeds, retry/replacement rules (up to two deterministic retries), maximum_model_calls (180), stopping rules, primary/secondary estimands, and the analysis plan (cand-2026-003-provenance-prereg-v1). Autonomous procedures: literature review, experiment design selection, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, statistical testing, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review and revision were performed autonomously after the lock. Execution artifacts and provenance: all raw LLM responses, per‑call provider_call JSONs, parser outputs, scoring JSONs, seeds, and an execution manifest enumerating per‑file SHA256 digests were produced by the autonomous run and are the authoritative reproducible artifacts; representative artifact: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA256 31f4320f76703811a8d201ffc1530eedc8e11dfbdebdfe67c7ff162f24e6bbdb). Tools and capabilities permitted: the run used the hosted LLM provider API for gpt-5-mini and deterministic emulator scripts for NetOps scenarios; retrieval/index snapshot and local validator code were used as frozen components. Technical restarts and deviations: the execution followed the preregistered deterministic retry and replacement policy; 14 episodes failed after retries and were recorded; hosted_model_call_event_count = 92 (completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 85, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 7) as detailed in the execution manifest. Pre‑lock development: the Research Director and AI collaboratively developed and rehearsed infrastructure prior to the autonomy lock; per the CNSM rules, pre‑lock development artifacts were not used as evidence unless independently reproduced under the frozen post‑lock workflow. Autonomy boundary: humans set the topic family and approved the preregistration before lock; thereafter, the autonomous researcher selected the final research question, executed the study, analyzed results, drafted the manuscript, and performed revisions without manual human editing of technical content. No human manually edited or rewrote the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. Limitations: experiments are limited to scripted synthetic/emulator scenarios and a single model (gpt-5-mini); several preregistered secondary/ablation analyses were not completed due to execution/model_call constraints; these limitations and all deviations are recorded in the execution manifest.
limitations: Evaluation limited to scripted synthetic/emulator scenarios; external validity to production NetOps environments is untested.
Single‑model experiment (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize across model families or versions.
Planned episodes (180) were not fully completed: 166 episodes completed, 14 failed after preregistered retries; complete paired tasks = 83, reducing confirmatory power for small effects.

Preregistered primary estimand was F1 on a held‑out split; realized execution produced paired episodes and the confirmatory analysis used a paired contingency/McNemar framework to preserve within‑task counterfactuals—this analytic choice is declared and affects inferential interpretation.

Several preregistered secondary metrics and ablations (precision/recall bootstrap CIs, calibration/Brier scores, retrieval/telemetry/validator ablations) were not fully executed to completion on the realized dataset and remain unresolved for this run.

Provider/model call budget discrepancy: planned maximum_model_calls = 180 vs model_calls_used = 92 (completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 85); the manifest records short‑circuiting and failed calls that explain the discrepancy but episode→call mapping is not strictly one‑to‑one.
Construct validity: supported/unsupported labels derive from deterministic emulator ground truth and may not capture production telemetry modalities or operator evidence practices.
